newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Naming of cabinet fuels Nicaragua vote controversy.
newsitem.headline: Naming of cabinet fuels Nicaragua vote controversy.

text.p: With his electoral victory still not official, Nicaragua's apparent president-elect Arnoldo Aleman already has named almost his entire cabinet despite simmering post-election tensions.

Twelve days after Nicaragua's presidential vote, election authorities have not announced the winners. Nevertheless, Aleman has named most of his cabinet to the chagrin of the rival, left-wing Sandinista Front, which has not recognised his victory.

"We have something very unique happening in Nicaragua. Before we even know the final results of the elections, we have a 'virtual president-elect' who has already started naming his cabinet," political analyst Carlos Tunnermann told Reuters on Friday. "In other countries they at least wait until the vote is counted or even until they take office."
Aleman on Friday called on the Sandinistas to concede defeat and end the uncertainty gripping the nation, but he also extended an olive branch, offering to work with them in the future.
"I think that for Nicaragua's sake we should begin the reconstruction process now. I invite the Sandinistas to help us rebuild Nicaragua," Aleman told reporters.

Preliminary results from Nicaragua's disputed Oct. 20 vote gave Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance a 49 percent to 38 percent lead over former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega with 87 percent of the vote counted.

But the Sandinistas and several small parties have charged the vote was riddled with "serious irregularities," hinting at Liberal fraud, and are waiting for Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council (CSE) to review the count.
The CSE has said the winners will not be announced until mid- or late-November.
The delay in announcing the winners, and charges of fraud and irresponsibility being thrown between the bitter political rivals, have threatened to spark social unrest.

The Sandinistas raised the political stakes late on Thursday when they called on the CSE to declare the elections null in the department (province) of Managua due to "massive inconsistencies" and hold a new vote.
Aleman's naming of a cabinet of prominent political figures was seen by some analysts as an attempt to legitimise his victory and make his presidency look like a done deal.

"I think he is doing it to satisfy the people that his victory is worthwhile, that defending it is worth the effort," Tunnermann said. "His appointments have been people with a high academic level, who enjoy prestige in their professions."
Tunnermann said Aleman's government was shaping up to be "center-right, with an inclination to the right."
Aleman has named Liberal congressman Jaime Cuadra Somarriba as Nicaragua's first civilian defence minister.
The appointment of Cuadra Somarriba, who was imprisoned by the dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza in the 1970s, is the first time a civilian has been put in charge of the army.

Other key appointments include economist Mario Alonso as finance minister, economist Noel Ramirez as central bank president, and Francisco Lainez, a former central bank president during the Somoza government, as economy minister.
